newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan economy shows signs of stabilising.
newsitem.headline: Angolan economy shows signs of stabilising.

text.p: - After 100 days in government Angola's new economic team has stabilised the national currency, improved business confidence and begun the task of rooting out public service corruption, economists say.
But ordinary Angolans, most of whom live beneath the poverty line fighting hyper inflation, remain the biggest victims of an economy which is still in disarray.

Angolan Prime Minister Franca van Dunem and his new economic team were sworn into government in June after President Jose Eduardo dos Santos sacked his previous government in a bid to prop up public confidence in his leadership.
At the time, he promised to implement an economic programme known as "Nova Vida" (New Life).
The programme began on July 1 with vigorous steps to end parallel money markets and curb the circulation of the U.S. dollar on the black market which was undermining the Angolan kwanza.

"By getting rid of the informal market the government has managed to stop the demand for the dollar on the parallel market," a Western economist said, noting the move had helped stabilise the kwanza at around 200,000 to the dollar for more than two months.
The government also introduced new rules that forced all import transactions to be conducted through the banking network.
And, as promised in his "New Life" speech, dos Santos has paid most of the public workers' salaries in arrears and increased the average wage from U.S.$20 to U.S.$40 a month.
"All these moves indicate the government is moving in the right direction which has won the support of business," another economist said.
One of the government's biggest challenges has been to clamp down on large scale corruption in the public service.
Economists believe that the government has made an important move to end corruption by halting the commercial activities of the national bank.
It transferred the bank's commercial activities to the state owned Caixa de Credito Agro-Pecuaria e Pescas, a move which economists say will put an end to a lot of corruption.
Crackdowns in the customs department by forcing traders to go through the commerce ministry and through banks to clear their goods was also one of the moves to end corruption.
Ordinary Angolans are still reeling, however, despite the fixing of prices of at least 50 basic product by the government.
Latest National Institute for Statistics figures show annual inflation rocketed over 1,300 percent in July from a 917 percent year-on-year increase in June.

"The ordinary Angolan is not feeling the positive changes. If the government does not give to the Angolan the power to buy these products, it won't make a difference to their lives," one economist said.
